tagline: Along the St. Johns, under oaks a governor saved.
intro: From the Julington Creek bridge at the county line, State Road 13 winds south about 17 miles along the east side of the St. Johns River to Ward's Creek, through pine and palmetto barrens, oak hammocks and swamps, much of it under moss-draped trees.

The trees nearly went. In 1997 the governor stepped in to stop the removal of centennial oaks along the highway, and local people set about getting it designated. The road carries the name of William Bartram, the naturalist who failed as a planter on this river in the 1760s and came back in 1774 on the journey he later told in his Travels.

moments.title: Julington Creek
moments.text: The road starts on a bridge over the creek where it widens into the St. Johns, and Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote about her visits here in Palmetto Leaves.

moments.title: Switzerland
moments.text: The name comes from Francis Philip Fatio's New Switzerland plantation, where Bartram landed in his little sailboat in 1774.

moments.title: Fort Picolata
moments.text: South of the byway, at the old river crossing, stood the Spanish fort near which Bartram had failed as a planter seven years before he came back by in 1774.
